Third port, and the first from Family B (Tribus). His source site is far
thinner than the Luxury Presence two: no neighbourhoods, no blog, no
valuation page, no stats. So this site is seven pages, not ten, and leans
on the brokerage pages the way the catalogue recommends. Two data-shape
differences absorbed by the builder rather than by hand: listing `specs` is
optional (his cards publish price + address + listing broker, no beds), and
`fit: contain` handles a cut-out studio headshot.

blocks.label: Residential, Commercial, Investment
blocks.title: Residential, commercial, investment.
blocks.lede: Most Steamboat agents do one of these. Doing all three is why {{agent.first}} gets called about the odd ones.
paragraphs: Steamboat's commercial and mixed-use inventory is small, rarely marketed widely, and priced on assumptions that are hard to check from outside. A downtown retail bay, a Copper Ridge industrial unit, a short-term-rental condominium underwritten on real occupancy rather than projected — these need someone who has actually closed them.

The residential half is the volume: first mountain homes, move-ups, second homes and luxury. Roughly half of {{agent.first}}'s recent closings were on the buy side, working against other brokerages' listings, which is worth knowing if you are the one buying.

blocks.label: Page header
blocks.title: The half of the market nobody markets.
blocks.lede: Steamboat's commercial and mixed-use inventory is small, traded quietly, and priced on assumptions that are hard to check from outside the valley.

blocks.label: How It Trades
blocks.title: Small inventory, thin comparables.
paragraphs: There are only so many retail bays on Lincoln Avenue, only so many industrial units at Copper Ridge, and in a given year only a handful of either changes hands. That means the comparable set for any commercial property here is small enough that a single unusual sale distorts it — and small enough that the people who closed those sales are the only reliable source on why the numbers looked the way they did.

The same is true of the investment side. A short-term-rental condominium is priced off projected income, and projections are where the optimism lives. {{agent.first}} underwrites on actual occupancy and actual expenses: management split, HOA reserves, cleaning, the shoulder seasons nobody models, and whether the licence transfers at all.

blocks.label: About These Reviews
blocks.title: Two notes on the set.
paragraphs: These come across from Testimonial Tree as written. Two things are worth naming rather than designing around.

First, more than half mention Geoff alongside {{agent.first}}. If that partnership is current, the site should say so plainly — a two-person team is a selling point, and reviews that name someone the site never introduces read as an oversight. If it is historic, the reviews are still true and the copy should place them in time.
Second, none carry a submarket or a transaction side. “Bryan Swintek · Mountain Area Buyer” would prove geographic range at the same time as it proves service, at the cost of one permission request.
checks: Decide whether the Geoff partnership is current, and say so
Add submarket and buy/sell side to each review
Date the older ones so the set reads as a fourteen-year record
Keep the short ones — “A+” is credible precisely because it is unpolished
